title: Science and faith
hook: physicist-priest John Polkinghorne saw science and faith as two windows

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Mbiti and African theology: a person as a thread in a cloth. Your line was I am because we are.

Why is the kettle boiling? One answer: the burner heats the water, the molecules speed up, and it turns to steam. Another: because I'd like a cup of tea. Both are true. Neither cancels the other. John Polkinghorne used that kitchen puzzle. He was a physicist who worked on the tiniest pieces of matter, the particles inside the atom. Then he left his professorship, trained for the ministry, and became an Anglican priest. You met another priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître, back in year three. Today's word is the two things Polkinghorne refused to choose between.

He didn't think science and faith were fighting over the same ground. Picture two windows in one house. His own phrase was binocular vision: two eyes, set a little apart, give depth that one eye can't. First window: science. It asks how. How do stars form? It tests, measures, and changes its mind when the evidence says so. He left research physics, but once ordained he kept writing about science for the rest of his life. Second window: faith. It asks why, and what for. Is there purpose? Is there love behind the light? The psalm looks up at the sky a physicist studies and sees more: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Third, where the windows meet. Polkinghorne was struck that the universe can be understood at all. Mathematics worked out on paper fits the way the world actually behaves. Why should it? For him, that was a clue: a world that makes sense, as if made by a mind. A hint worth following, he said, not a proof. Fourth, humility on both sides. Science says, we don't know yet, let's look. Faith at its best says something similar. Gazing at the night sky, the psalmist asks: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Not an answer. Wonder. Polkinghorne thought a scientist and a believer could share it, and one person could be both.

Pick one thing you can see, a plant, your hand, a cup, and look through the how window: what is it made of, how does it work? Then, slowly, the why window: what is it for, what does it mean to you, is anything in it worth thanking someone for? If you pray, offer that thanks to God; if not, let both views sit side by side.
Science and faith. For John Polkinghorne, two windows on one world: one asks how, the other asks why, and together they give depth.
Your line: two windows. One world, and the depth comes from looking through both. See you tomorrow.
